blogs.title: Intrinsic vs. Propensity: The Eighth Circuit Reaffirms the 'Continuous Possession' Doctrine in Firearm Cases
blogs.description: This post analyzes the appellate court's handling of the Rule 404(b) challenge regarding testimony that the defendant had possessed the specific sawed-off rifle on previous occasions. While defendants often argue such testimony is improper character evidence intended to show bad acts, the Eighth Circuit's reliance on *United States v. Battle* clarifies that proof of prior possession of the exact same weapon is 'intrinsic' to establishing current control and ownership. The article explores how this distinction narrows the scope of admissible evidence for prosecutors in felon-in-possession cases, effectively allowing them to introduce a history of interaction with the specific firearm without triggering strict propensity prohibitions.

blogs.title: The Silent Record: Appellate Review Standards and the Burden of Preservation in Evidentiary Challenges
blogs.description: Focusing on Section II(D) and (E) of the opinion, this blog examines the high bar for reversing evidentiary rulings when a defendant fails to adequately preserve arguments or cite controlling authority. The court explicitly rebukes Cutbank for raising claims without supporting case law and notes that even unpreserved errors are subject to plain error review, which requires showing obviousness and prejudice. This post discusses the practical implications for defense counsel, highlighting how failure to object specifically to authentication requirements for extrinsic impeachment evidence or failing to articulate Rule 403 prejudice can lead to automatic affirmation regardless of potential trial irregularities.

blogs.title: ACCA Overload: Navigating Conflicting Guidelines Enhancements Under § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B)
blogs.description: This piece dissects the sentencing calculation where the district court applied a four-level enhancement for possessing a firearm 'in connection with another felony offense.' The author analyzes Cutbank's argument that applying this enhancement alongside an Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA) sentence creates a conflict with 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a)'s requirement that sentences be 'sufficient but not greater than necessary.' The discussion centers on why the Eighth Circuit found no error, noting that while ACCA triggers mandatory minimums, it does not preclude additional guideline enhancements if they result in a higher offense level under USSG § 4B1.4(b). The post concludes by exploring how courts balance statutory mandates against discretionary sentencing factors when multiple aggravating circumstances overlap.
